Introducing Lumma-Fev-v2

Community Article Published
October 29, 2026 Upvote 15 Rohit rohitsali FrontiersMind Vishesh Tripathi vishesh-t27 FrontiersMind Abhay kumar akanyaani FrontiersMind Ramsha ramshakhann FrontiersMind
The second generation of our Lumma-Fev decision models: one family from 0.1B to 27B, one forward pass, nothing to parse.

f asking a model to make a decision end the same way: the model writes a sentence, and your code tries to read it. A label comes back with extra words, a number comes back as text, and a confidence is whatever the model feels like saying.
Lumma-Fev-v2 is a family of decision models that skips that step. You give a model a state and typed questions, and it returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. It never generates text, so there is nothing to parse.
The family covers every size you might need, from small models built on our own Nandi-Mini and Lumma base models up to Qwen3.8-27B, and every size shares one interface. Today we are releasing Lumma-Fev-4B-v2 and Lumma-Fev-27B-v2, with 0.1B and 0.6B models coming soon.
Both released models score higher than TypeSafe Jev 1.13.0 on average across eight public benchmarks, and both are better calibrated. Where Jev still leads, we say so below.
👉 Models: Lumma-Fev-0.1B-v2 · Lumma-Fev-4B-v2 · Lumma-Fev-27B-v2

A Decision Model, Not a Generator

Each Lumma-Fev model takes a state, which can be text, a JSON object or an array, plus a set of typed questions. It scores every option of every question at once and hands the probabilities back. Because the answer is a distribution and not a sentence, you can set a threshold, route on the top option, or send low-confidence cases to a person.

One call, two questions. The model reads the state and both questions together and returns a probability for each option. Bar lengths are illustrative.

One Family, Four Sizes

Every Lumma-Fev decision model is a fine-tune of a pretrained base model. The small ones start from our own Nandi-Mini and Lumma foundation models, the larger ones from Qwen. The interface does not change between them, so you can prototype on a small model and move up, or down, without touching your code.

What Changed in v2

Lumma-Fev-27B-v2 is the flagship of the family and the successor to Lumma-Fev-27B. Three things are different.

Bidirectional Attention

In Lumma-Fev-27B-v2, the full-attention layers read the whole prompt in both directions, like an encoder. The Gated DeltaNet (linear-attention) layers stay causal. For a decision model that is a natural fit: the state and the questions are all in the prompt before any answer is scored, so there is no reason for an early token to be blind to a later one.

Attention over eight tokens. Filled cells are the positions a token can read. In Lumma-Fev-27B-v2 the full-attention layers are bidirectional, and the Gated DeltaNet layers stay causal.

Because of this, the checkpoint needs lumma-fev 0.3 or later. Older versions do not apply bidirectional attention and refuse to load it.

3× the Training Data

Lumma-Fev-27B-v2 trains on about 300K samples, up from about 100K for v1.

Trained With decisionformer

We trained the Lumma-Fev-v2 models with decisionformer, our open-source (Apache 2.0) library for fine-tuning, loading and serving calibrated decision models on any Hugging Face model. It supports full, LoRA, QLoRA and head-only fine-tuning through YAML recipes, with a CLI and multi-GPU support, and it includes tools to evaluate and compare checkpoints and push them to the Hub. If you want to train your own decision model, start there.

The Same Interface as v1

Every Lumma-Fev-v2 model uses the interface of v1, so nothing changes for existing users. Each model takes a state (text, a JSON object or an array) and a set of typed questions:

noul: a yes/no-style question about the state, such as "Does the customer need a reply today?"
choice: pick one option from labeled criteria, with a probability for each.
score: accepted, but untested. The models were trained on noul and choice questions only.

Each answer comes back with its type, the choice, a confidence, and the full probabilities over every option.
Languages: English, Hindi, Tamil and Kannada, plus Hinglish.

Accuracy in percent. Best in each row in bold.
The 0.1B model, built on our own Nandi-Mini-150M, shows how much a very small model can do. It scores 93.2% on Emotion, the highest of any model in the chart, and it is ahead of Jev on AG News (89.9 against 89.2) and BANKING77 (85.3 against 79.5). On the tasks that need more reading and reasoning it is far behind, with 41.7 on Financial PhraseBank, 37.7 on RAGTruth and 35.9 on BBH, so its average is 60.4%, against 81.2% for Jev. The weights are at FrontiersMind/Lumma-fev-0.1B-v2.

Confidence You Can Read

A decision model is only useful for automation if its probabilities mean something. Both Lumma-Fev-v2 models beat Jev on log loss, ECE and Brier, and Lumma-Fev-27B-v2 is the best calibrated of the three on every metric.
The reliability diagram shows it directly. Each point is a confidence bin, and the closer a point sits to the dotted diagonal, the more the model's stated confidence matches how often it is right. The two Lumma-Fev-v2 models follow the diagonal closely, while Jev sits below it: when Jev says 90%, it is right about 80% of the time.

Eight benchmarks pooled, 11,657 rows, 15 equal-width confidence bins. Confidence is the top option's probability after temperature scaling. Each point is a bin with at least 20 rows, and its size grows with the number of rows. The dotted line is perfect calibration. ECE is on the pooled rows.
On the pooled rows, the calibration error (ECE) is 0.004 for Lumma-Fev-4B-v2, 0.010 for Lumma-Fev-27B-v2 and 0.065 for Lumma-Fev-0.1B-v2, against 0.091 for Jev. Test It Yourself

Install

pip install "lumma-fev>=0.3"

Version 0.3 or later is required to load Lumma-Fev-27B-v2, because it uses bidirectional attention.

Python

import lumma_fev

model = lumma_fev.load("FrontiersMind/Lumma-fev-27B-v2") # or lumma_fev.load("27b-v2")
# model = lumma_fev.load("FrontiersMind/Lumma-fev-4B-v2") # smaller model, same interface
# model = lumma_fev.load("27b-v2", device_map="auto") # several GPUs: pip install "lumma-fev[large]"

answers = model.decide(
state="My integration keeps failing. Please help.",
questions={
"team": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which team should handle this request?",
"criteria": {
"billing": "Charges and refunds",
"support": "Technical integration errors",
"sales": "Questions about buying a product",
},
},
"urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the customer need a reply today?"},
},
)
print(answers["team"])
# {"type": "choice", "choice": "support", "confidence": 0.99..., "probabilities": {"billing": ..., "support": ..., "sales": ...}}

Images

Install the extra and pass images=[...] (paths, PIL images or data: URLs):
pip install "lumma-fev[images]"

HTTP API

To serve a model behind the TypeSafe-compatible POST /v1/systemone API:
pip install "lumma-fev[serve]"
lumma-fev-serve --model 27b-v2 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 # add --device-map auto for several GPUs

Requirements and Limits

GPU memory (27B-v2): about 55 GB free (a single 80 GB card), or several smaller GPUs with device_map="auto".
Precision: BF16, Safetensors.
Context: a question plus the state must fit in 8,192 tokens.
score questions: accepted but untested.
Loading 27B-v2 weights yourself: decision_config.json has "attention_mode": "noncausal_full_attention". Set config.is_causal = False on the text config and is_causal = False on every text attention module after loading. Setting only the config makes single unpadded requests run causally.

What's Next

Lumma-Fev-0.1B-v2 and Lumma-Fev-0.6B-v2 are coming soon, built on Nandi-Mini-150M and Lumma-0.6B-Base. Jev still leads on BBH and JudgeBench, so reasoning remains the main gap for the family.
Try the Lumma-Fev-v2 models on your own decisions, and tell us where they fail. Those failures shape the next version. To fine-tune your own decision model, use decisionformer.
